source.title: Modulating Cross-Modal Convergence with Single-Stimulus, Intra-Modal Dispersion
source.authors: Eghbal A. Hosseini; Brian Cheung; Evelina Fedorenko; Alex H. Williams

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-modal alignment under different stimulus-selection conditions and reports that stimulus dispersion substantially changes the alignment, refining the claim by showing dependence on the inputs.
record.gate_note: The study reports cross-modal alignment for stimulus subsets selected by dispersion and for subsets formed by excluding stimuli. The main figures show individual model pairings, but the text also states qualitative aggregate patterns across all tested pairings; rows below record only those aggregate statements. Exact values for individual pairings are presented only in figures. The supplementary held-out-model dispersion correlations concern prediction of intra-modal deviation, not cross-modal alignment, so they are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures vision–language CKNNA alignment on WIT image-caption pairs under different stimulus subsets. It shows the measured cross-modal convergence changes, up to twofold, with which inputs are used. This bears directly on V6's claim that convergence depends on the inputs.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that stimuli with low dispersion across vision models (high intra-modal agreement) give markedly higher vision–language alignment, up to about twofold. They say the effect is robust to two selection criteria and generalizes across pairings. They frame this as a stricter, stimulus-level test of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, not as evidence against it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses generalized Procrustes analysis to select stimuli by intra-modal dispersion and CKNNA (k=10) to measure cross-modal alignment; it does not test convergence as a function of model scale or capability.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment changes with stimulus selection: rank-based mean dispersion, PC1-based dispersion, and exclusion of high- versus low-dispersion stimuli produce different alignment levels.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-stimulus dispersion computed from three vision models predicts the held-out fourth model's deviation from consensus (Pearson r = 0.21–0.43, all p<0.001).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intra-modal convergence varies by stimulus in a way shared across vision models with different objectives.

record.peer_reviewed: To appear at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align)
record.problems: The alignment experiment uses one dataset of 1024 image-caption pairs and one reported CKNNA setting (k=10). Main alignment values are shown in figures, while the text gives qualitative aggregate comparisons rather than exact values or uncertainty estimates for those comparisons. No alternative alignment metric or out-of-distribution dataset is tested.
record.rows_left_out: Individual vision–language pairing values plotted in Figure 2B-E, Figure 2G-J, and Supplementary Figure S1 were not transcribed; the text supplies aggregate qualitative statements, and the 60-row cap is not reached. Supplementary Figure S2 concerns held-out intra-modal deviation rather than cross-modal alignment.

untested.parts: No test of whether alignment rises with model scale or capability. Alignment is plotted against LLM size, but the text draws no scale trend.
Image-caption alignment is measured, but the text never examines whether it rises as vision or language models improve.
No stitching, mapping-loss or relative-representation tests. GPA is used only to compute dispersion.
No feature- or circuit-level universality test.
Only the input dimension is tested. There are no alternative similarity metrics, no variation of k (only k=10) and no out-of-distribution data.
No test of plateau or of shared data or objectives as causes.

missing.what: Per-pairing alignment values across LLM sizes (560m–65b) for each stimulus set. These could show whether alignment rises with language-model scale and whether that trend survives on high-dispersion stimuli. Shown only in figures, not stated in the text.
Number of stimuli in the low, high and random sets for Fig 2. This matters because CKNNA on subsets of different size may not be comparable.

record.verdict_notes: This is a short workshop paper. Brian Cheung is a co-author of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis paper, but this study is not itself an original source, so verdicts are allowed. Subset selection uses vision-model agreement, and the outcome is vision–language agreement, so the effect partly reflects choosing stimuli where vision representations are consistent. No uncertainty estimates are given for the alignment comparisons despite the word 'significantly'.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether alignment between independently trained models rises with model scale or capability.
It measures image-caption alignment across model pairings, but does not test whether alignment rises as both models become better.
No comparison across initialization seeds of the same architecture.
No test of interchangeability, layer stitching, relative representations, or unpaired mappings.
No test for recurring interpretable features or circuits.

The study tests dependence on the selected stimuli and on two stimulus-selection strategies. It does not compare alternative alignment metrics or k settings, and does not test out-of-distribution inputs.
It does not test whether alignment plateaus or whether shared data or objectives explain it.

relationships.condition: WIT 1024 pairs; 4 ViT vision models × 12 BLOOM/OpenLLaMA/LLaMA models; CKNNA k=10; subsets chosen or dropped by vision-model dispersion
relationships.reason: Alignment rises up to twofold on low-dispersion subsets and falls on high-dispersion ones (R1, R2). Dropping low-dispersion stimuli lowers alignment below the full set across all pairings (R3, R4).
relationships.display_finding: Low-dispersion subsets increased alignment up to twofold, high-dispersion subsets reduced it, and removing low-dispersion stimuli lowered alignment below the full-set value across all model pairings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
